course.description: Move vectors, reshape a plane and fit noisy measurements. Build up to eigenvectors and singular value decomposition.

lessons.title: Read a vector

blocks.text: Read the first coordinate
A vector records an ordered list of coordinates. In the plane, the first coordinate measures horizontal movement and the second measures vertical movement.
Keep the order
Changing the order changes the vector. The pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) point to different locations.
Find the zero vector
The zero vector has every coordinate equal to zero. Its length is zero; it stays at the origin.
Read a coordinate direction
The standard coordinate vectors are (1, 0) and (0, 1). They give one unit of movement along just one axis.

lessons.orientation: Read signed coordinates and distinguish vectors from individual scalars.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Add and scale vectors

blocks.text: Combine displacements
Vector addition combines matching coordinates. Add horizontal movements to horizontal movements and vertical movements to vertical movements.
Stretch both coordinates
A scalar multiplies every coordinate. Scaling by 3 triples the length and keeps the direction.
Reverse the direction
A negative scalar reverses the vector's direction. Its absolute value determines the factor by which length changes.
Cancel a displacement
Every vector has an additive inverse. Adding a vector to its negative produces the zero vector.

lessons.orientation: Combine displacements, scale every coordinate and handle negative scalars.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Dot products and length

blocks.text: Combine matching products
The dot product is one scalar. Multiply corresponding entries and add the products.
Measure the length
The squared length of a vector equals its dot product with itself. Take the nonnegative square root to obtain the length.
Square before adding
A vector's dot product with itself cannot be negative. Each matching-coordinate product is a square.
Ignore the signs in length
Changing signs can change a direction while preserving its length. Squaring removes each coordinate's sign.

lessons.orientation: Use matching-coordinate products to measure alignment and vector length.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Orthogonal and unit vectors

blocks.text: Test perpendicular directions
Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero. For nonzero plane vectors, this means their directions are perpendicular.
Keep direction, set length to one
Divide a nonzero vector by its length to obtain a unit vector in the same direction. For (3, 4), divide each coordinate by 5.
Separate two conditions
Orthogonal vectors do not have to be unit vectors. An orthonormal set must satisfy both perpendicularity and length one.
Respect the zero exception
The zero vector has no direction and cannot be normalised by dividing by its length. Division by zero is undefined.

lessons.orientation: Recognise perpendicular vectors and turn a nonzero vector into a unit vector.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Matrix shape and transpose

blocks.text: Read the shape
A matrix's shape gives its row count followed by its column count. This example has two rows and three columns.
Count the input coordinates
A matrix with three columns multiplies a vector with three entries. The output has one entry for each matrix row.
Swap row and column
Transposition moves entry (i, j) to position (j, i). It changes a two-by-three matrix into a three-by-two matrix.
Transpose the shape
Transposing swaps the shape's dimensions. Doing it twice returns the original entries and shape.

lessons.orientation: Read rows and columns, transpose entries and check input dimensions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Linear transformations

blocks.text: Weight the columns
The entries of v weight the columns of A. Equivalently, each output entry is the dot product of one matrix row with v.
Read a basis image
Multiplying by (1, 0) selects the first column. The columns tell us where the coordinate directions go.
Preserve addition and scaling
A linear map preserves sums and scalar multiples: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v), and T(cu) = cT(u). Every matrix map has these properties.
Test the origin
The translation S(v) = v + (1, 0) sends the origin to (1, 0), so it is not linear. Sending zero to zero is necessary for linearity, but is not sufficient by itself.

lessons.orientation: Apply a matrix and distinguish linear maps from translations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Compose matrix maps

blocks.text: Use a row and a column
Each product entry combines a row of A with a column of B. For the top-right entry, use the first row of A and second column of B.
Reverse the order
Matrix multiplication generally depends on order. Switching the maps can change the output even when both products exist.
Match the inner dimensions
A two-by-three matrix can multiply a three-by-two matrix. The matching inner dimensions disappear; the result has two rows and two columns.
Read the composition
In A B v, B acts on v first. A then acts on that intermediate output.

lessons.orientation: Multiply compatible matrices and keep the order of composition.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Identity and inverses

blocks.text: Leave a vector unchanged
The identity matrix has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere. It leaves every vector unchanged and is its own inverse.
Undo the whole map
An inverse must undo all parts of the map. For a square invertible A, both A⁻¹A and AA⁻¹ equal I.
Notice lost information
The columns (1, 2) and (2, 4) lie on one line. This square map collapses different inputs to the same output and has no inverse.
Recover an input
If A is invertible, A v = b has the unique solution v = A⁻¹b. You can check the recovered input by applying A again.

lessons.orientation: Undo an invertible square map and recognise when an inverse cannot exist.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Solve by row reduction

blocks.text: Keep both sides together
The augmented matrix places the right side beside the coefficients. Swapping equations, scaling a row by a nonzero number, or adding a multiple of another row preserves the solution set.
Eliminate a variable
Subtract twice the first equation from the second. Apply this operation to every entry, including the right side.
Make a pivot equal one
After elimination, the second equation is −3x₂ = −9. Divide both sides by −3 to read the value of x₂.
Swap when needed
A zero in the first pivot position may require swapping rows. It does not by itself mean the matrix is singular.

lessons.orientation: Use equivalent row operations to solve A x = b and check the result.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: One, none or many solutions

blocks.text: Read a unique solution
A consistent system with a pivot in every variable column has one solution. Here the equations specify both coordinates directly.
Find a contradiction
An equation that reduces to 0 = 1 cannot be satisfied. A contradiction makes the entire system inconsistent.
Leave a free variable
When one equation is redundant, a variable may remain free. A consistent real system with a free variable has infinitely many solutions.
Count free variables
The number of free variables equals the number of variable columns minus the rank. The right-hand column does not represent another variable.

lessons.orientation: Classify systems using contradictions, pivots and free variables.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Spans and subspaces

blocks.text: Follow one line
Multiples of one nonzero vector fill a line through the origin. Adding another vector on that same line does not enlarge the span.
Reach the plane
Two independent plane vectors span the entire plane. Their linear combinations can move in two independent directions.
Keep zero and closure
A subspace contains zero and stays inside itself under addition and scalar multiplication. A line y = 2x through the origin satisfies these conditions.
Check an offset
The line y = 2x + 1 excludes the origin. This offset prevents it from being a subspace.

lessons.orientation: Describe all linear combinations and test the conditions for a subspace.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Basis and dimension

blocks.text: Remove redundancy
A basis spans a space and is linearly independent. In the plane, the two standard coordinate vectors form a basis.
Spanning is not enough
The vectors (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, 1) span the plane, but the third is the sum of the first two. A basis cannot contain that redundancy.
Change the coordinates
Coordinates depend on the chosen basis. For the ordered basis ((1, 1), (1, −1)), coordinates (3, 1) describe the usual vector (4, 2).
Exclude zero from a basis
A set containing the zero vector is dependent: multiplying that vector by a nonzero coefficient still gives zero. It cannot be a basis.

lessons.orientation: Find a spanning independent set and use its vectors as coordinates.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Rank and null space

blocks.text: Count independent outputs
The rank equals the dimension of the column space. Row reduction finds it by counting pivots in the coefficient columns.
Count hidden input directions
For a matrix with n columns, rank + nullity = n. The null space consists of all inputs that A sends to zero.
Test a null vector
An input belongs to the null space if multiplying it by A gives the zero vector. Such directions disappear from the output.
Keep the original columns
Pivot positions identify a basis for the column space using the original matrix's columns. Row operations may change those column vectors, so keep the originals.

lessons.orientation: Connect pivot columns, column space and the inputs a matrix sends to zero.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Determinants and volume

blocks.text: Measure an area factor
For a two-by-two matrix [(a, b); (c, d)], the determinant is ad − bc. Its absolute value gives the factor by which the map changes area.
Track orientation
Swapping two rows reverses the determinant's sign. A negative determinant reverses orientation while its absolute value still scales area.
Detect a collapse
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Dependent columns collapse area or volume and give determinant zero.
Move into three dimensions
For a three-dimensional map, the absolute determinant scales volume. A diagonal map scales its coordinate directions independently.

lessons.orientation: Read signed area and volume factors and use zero determinant to detect collapse.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Project onto a direction

blocks.text: Find the closest point on a line
The projection of v onto a nonzero direction d is ((v · d)/(d · d))d. The projected point lies on the line spanned by d.
Keep the same line
Rescaling a nonzero direction vector does not change the projection line or projected point.
Measure what remains
Subtract the projection from v to get the residual. It is perpendicular to the direction used for the projection.
Handle perpendicular input
If v is already perpendicular to the line, its projection is zero. The closest point on that line is the origin.

lessons.orientation: Find the closest vector on a line and a perpendicular residual.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Fit with least squares

blocks.text: Fit a noisy constant
One constant cannot exactly equal measurements 2, 4 and 9 at once. The least-squares constant is their mean, which minimises the sum of squared differences.
Read the perpendicular residual
Least squares makes the residual b − A x perpendicular to every column of A. For a constant fit, this means the residual entries sum to zero.
Fit a line
For y ≈ c + sx, put a column of ones beside the x values. The fitting coefficients minimise squared error; full column rank makes those coefficients unique.
Square the residuals
Squared error adds squares, so negative and positive residuals cannot cancel each other's cost. This differs from adding the residuals themselves.

lessons.orientation: Fit inconsistent measurements by minimising squared residuals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Build an orthonormal basis

blocks.text: Remove the shared direction
Gram–Schmidt subtracts the projection onto an earlier direction. The residual is perpendicular to that direction and keeps the span when the original vectors are independent.
Set the first length
Normalise the first nonzero direction. Dividing (1, 1) by its length gives each unit coordinate 1/√2.
Check orthogonality
After removing the projection, normalise the residual. These steps produce perpendicular unit vectors; their dot product is zero.
Stop at a redundant vector
A dependent input produces a zero residual after its earlier components are removed. You cannot normalise it to create an additional basis direction.

lessons.orientation: Subtract projections and normalise the remaining independent directions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues

blocks.text: Keep one line
An eigenvector is nonzero and satisfies A v = λv. Its output stays on the same line, and λ is its eigenvalue.
Find another direction
The same matrix can have different eigenvalues on different eigenvector directions. The direction matters.
Allow a reversal
A negative eigenvalue reverses the direction along the eigenvector's line. Eigenvalues need not be positive.
Reject a changed line
The vector (1, 0) is sent to (2, 1) by this matrix. That output is not a scalar multiple of the input, so the candidate is not an eigenvector.

lessons.orientation: Find nonzero directions that a square map changes only by a scalar.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Diagonalise a map

blocks.text: Use eigenvector coordinates
If the columns of P are independent eigenvectors, A = P D P⁻¹. D contains their eigenvalues in the same column order.
Repeat a scaling
For an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ, applying A twice multiplies the vector by λ². Diagonalisation makes higher powers simpler too.
Require enough directions
A square real matrix can be diagonalised over the reals only when it has a basis of real eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue alone does not guarantee enough independent directions.
Match the order
Reordering P's eigenvector columns also reorders D's matching eigenvalues. Keep each direction paired with its own scale.

lessons.orientation: Use an eigenvector basis to separate a square map into independent scalings.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

lessons.title: Singular value decomposition

blocks.text: Read nonnegative stretches
The singular value decomposition is A = U Σ Vᵀ. Singular values are nonnegative stretch factors, even when A reverses a direction.
Keep a rectangular middle
Every real rectangular matrix has an SVD. In the full form for an m-by-n matrix, U is m-by-m, Σ is m-by-n, and Vᵀ is n-by-n.
Notice a missing stretch
The number of positive singular values equals the rank. A rank-one two-by-two map has one positive singular value and one zero singular value.
Separate the jobs
U and V are orthogonal: they preserve lengths while changing axes by rotations or reflections. Σ performs the stretching. Use the phase controls after feedback to follow these jobs separately.

lessons.orientation: Separate a rectangular map into orthogonal coordinate changes and nonnegative stretches.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.
